title: UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer Says Goodbye in His Final Question Time—With Jokes and Tears
summary: Have you ever had to say goodbye to a job you loved? That’s what happened to UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer on Wednesday. He stood up in the House of Commons for his final Prime Minister’s Questions—a weekly session where MPs ask the PM anything. But this time, instead of tough questions, there were jokes, kind words, and even some tears. Starmer told everyone it was “the end of my political journey” and that he was proud of what he’d done. He thanked his staff, saying they were “prepared to walk through fire for me.” When he left the room, his own MPs gave him a standing ovation—and many from other parties clapped too. His family watched from a balcony. The Chancellor, Rachel Reeves, looked like she might cry. Another Labour MP, Carolyn Harris, got emotional and said, “Every day we see his decency and his courage shine through.” Even the leader of the other party, Conservative Kemi Badenoch, didn’t attack him. She praised his work helping Ukraine and his friendship with its president. There were also light moments: jokes about England’s World Cup hopes and a local election. But it started on a sad note, remembering a former MP who had died. Starmer is stepping down after only two years as PM—his own party pushed him out. He’ll hand over power to Andy Burnham on Monday, after a special Labour conference on Friday. For a man known as “Mr. Rules,” it was a surprisingly warm goodbye.
why_it_matters: Even powerful leaders have to say goodbye, and the way people treat you when you leave shows what they really thought of your work—something that can happen with a class president or a team captain, too.

background_read: Keir Starmer (the UK's prime minister from 2024 to 2026) became the leader after the Labour Party won a general election, but he faced disagreements within his own party.
The House of Commons is where elected MPs debate and make laws. Every Wednesday, the prime minister must answer their questions in a tradition called Prime Minister’s Questions.
Andy Burnham (the mayor of Manchester) was chosen by Labour members to become the new leader, and Starmer will hand over power after a special party conference.

WHAT: Starmer faced his final Prime Minister’s Questions, which turned into a warm goodbye with jokes, tears, and a standing ovation, before stepping down as prime minister
WHERE: Inside the House of Commons in London, with his family watching from a balcony
WHY: His own Labour Party pushed him out after only two years, choosing a new leader to try to improve the party’s chances in future elections
